overview.title: The Fantastic Four, decade by decade
overview.lede: This is where Marvel starts. Not figuratively — Fantastic Four #1 in November 1961 is the first comic of the company as anyone now understands it, and almost everything else on this site is downstream of it. The tension that has driven the book ever since is right there in the premise: it is a science-fiction exploration comic and a domestic drama about four people who cannot get along, and every era on this shelf is an argument about which of those two it should mostly be.

sections.h: Four people who argue, in a comic with no costumes
body: The first issue has no costumes and no secret identities. They are four people who went up in a rocket, came back wrong, and are extremely annoyed about it — the Thing in particular spends the early years genuinely furious, and Reed is at fault, and the book says so.

That is the innovation, and it is easy to under-rate sixty years later: the superheroes bicker. Before this, teams got along. Marvel's whole later personality — flawed heroes, arguments, consequences — is being invented in real time in these issues.
Doctor Doom arrives in #5 and is immediately the best villain in comics: a rival rather than a monster, a head of state, and someone whose grudge against Reed is intellectual vanity rather than evil.

fig.cap: Left: #1, November 1961 — no costumes, a monster, and a cover that reads like a 1950s giant-creature comic, because that is what Marvel had been publishing. Right: #5, and Doom.

sections.h: The imperial phase, and it is the best superhero comic ever made
body: For roughly three years in the middle of the 1960s, Lee and Jack Kirby produced new ideas at a rate the medium has never matched. In about thirty issues: the Inhumans, the Negative Zone, the Black Panther, Galactus, the Silver Surfer, Annihilus, the Kree, and Franklin Richards.
#48–50, the Galactus trilogy, is the high-water mark — a world-eating god and his herald, arriving as a genuine cosmic event, and resolved by a moral argument rather than a punch.

#51, This Man... This Monster! is the one working comics writers name. It is a single issue about an imposter taking the Thing's place, and it ends on a self-sacrifice from a character introduced twenty pages earlier. It has been called the best superhero comic ever published more times than any other single issue.
#52 introduces the Black Panther — the first Black superhero in mainstream American comics, in July 1966, months before the Black Panther Party took the name.

fig.cap: Left: the Coming of Galactus. Right: #51 — the cover is the Thing standing in a machine room and the title is a sentence. No fight on it at all.

makers.b: Two things to look for. Kirby Krackle — the field of black dots he used to draw cosmic energy, which he invented here and which every artist since has borrowed. And the collage pages: real photographs and cut paper pasted into the Negative Zone sequences, because he wanted somewhere that did not look drawn.

The most consequential inker in Marvel history and almost never discussed. Sinnott's slick, rounded finish is what made Kirby's pencils look polished rather than raw — put a pre-Sinnott issue beside a post-Sinnott one and the book looks like it changed publisher.

sections.h: Kirby leaves, and the book spends a decade being good instead of great
body: Kirby left after #102 in 1970 for DC, where he did the Fourth World. He was not replaced so much as succeeded — by John Buscema, whose work here is beautiful, classical figure drawing and consciously not an impersonation.

The 1970s FF is a well-made superhero comic that has stopped inventing things at the same rate, and it knows it. Roy Thomas, Gerry Conway, Len Wein and Marv Wolfman all take turns; the book leans on its history more than any Marvel title had needed to before, because it was the first to have that much.
George Pérez arrives in the mid-70s, and the FF is exactly the book for him — four characters with wildly different visual problems, a supporting cast, and a lot of machinery.

fig.cap: Left: #102, Kirby's last. Right: #176 — the issue where the FF visit the Marvel offices, which is the decade's self-awareness in one cover.

sections.h: John Byrne, alone, for five years
body: Byrne wrote and drew it, which is the whole thing. A single sensibility for five years, with no writer/artist negotiation in the middle, and it is the only run since Kirby's that is talked about in the same breath.

His method was archaeology: go back through twenty years of the book, find the threads Lee and Kirby dropped, and pull them. The Negative Zone gets developed properly. Doom gets a solo issue (#258) that is simply a day in his life in Latveria and is one of the best villain stories anyone has written. Sue Richards stops being the one who turns invisible and becomes the most powerful person on the team.

It is also where the book is at its most domestic. Marriage, a child, a miscarriage (#267), a team member leaving because he is unhappy. Byrne treats the FF as a family drama that happens to be able to visit other dimensions, and that reading has been the default ever since.

fig.cap: Left: Byrne's first, #232. Right: #258 — a Doom solo issue whose cover is a hand and a doll's house.

makers.b: Look at his page layouts. Byrne is a rigorous, almost architectural storyteller — regular grids, deliberate panel counts, and splash pages held back until they mean something. After the 1970s' looseness it reads as enormously controlled, and it is why his quiet issues work.

sections.h: The sixteen years the shelf cannot show you
body: Fantastic Four #296–488 has never been collected in omnibus, so the shelf jumps from 1986 to 2002 — the whole Steve Englehart and Tom DeFalco stretch, Walter Simonson's much-loved short run, the 1996 Heroes Reborn year, and the Chris Claremont issues after it.
It is the largest hole on any shelf on this site, and it is Marvel's doing rather than a curation choice. If the next volume feels like it starts a long way from the last one, that is why.

sections.h: Two reboots of the tone: warm, then enormous
body: Mark Waid and Mike Wieringo take it back to first principles — explorers and a family — and write the run most people now name as the best modern FF. Unthinkable makes Doom genuinely frightening again by moving him from science to sorcery, and the book around it is funny and generous.

It also produced the shelf's most extraordinary piece of publishing history: in 2003 Marvel fired Waid and Wieringo over a creative disagreement, the news broke online, the fan reaction was severe enough to crash the site that reported it, and within weeks they were reinstated. It is one of very few times readers have visibly reversed an editorial decision.

Mark Millar and Bryan Hitch then do the opposite: widescreen, blockbuster, enormous set pieces drawn at maximum detail. Hitch's method — photo-real crowds, cinematic staging, panels shaped like film frames — is the house style of that decade at Marvel.

fig.cap: Left: Waid and Wieringo's #500. Right: Hitch, composing for a screen.

sections.h: Hickman builds a machine; Fraction takes the kids on holiday
body: Jonathan Hickman's run is the most architecturally ambitious thing anyone has done with these characters. It is planned years out, it is about Reed Richards' arrogance as a structural problem rather than a character note, and it culminates in the Council of Reeds — a room full of alternate Reeds who all made the same choice, which is the sharpest critique of the character ever put on paper.
#587 is where a member of the team dies and the book renames itself FF — and the issue shipped polybagged, which tells you how much Marvel thought it mattered.

Matt Fraction follows with a deliberately lighter idea: the family goes on a time-travelling holiday and a substitute team minds the Future Foundation children at home. Michael Allred draws the substitutes, in flat, pop-art, mid-century line work that looks like nothing else Marvel was printing.

fig.cap: Left: Hickman's first issue. Right: #587 — a solid-black cover with a number 3 on it.

sections.h: Slott puts the family back together
body: The book had been cancelled outright for three years — the longest the Fantastic Four have been off the shelf since 1961 — and Dan Slott relaunched it in 2018 on a straightforwardly restorative brief: get them back, get them married, make it warm.
It is the least formally adventurous era on this shelf and the most openly affectionate, which after Hickman's architecture and Fraction's experiments is a defensible thing to be.

fig.cap: The 2018 relaunch. The cover is the logo and the family.

sections.h: The two books that are not the team's
body: Ultimate Fantastic Four restarts them as very young scientists in a government think tank — Bendis, Millar and Adam Kubert, and it is the most accessible version of the concept anyone has produced. It is also where Marvel Zombies came from, which nobody planned.

And The Book of Doom is on the shelf because Doctor Doom is the reason half this book works. Reading fifteen years of him assembled out of the runs above shows something the monthly never quite does: he is almost never wrong about Reed, only about himself.

fig.cap: Left: Ultimate FF. Right: the Thing's own title, 1983 — the other side book on this shelf.

tone.sub: Nineteen books, and the FF swings further between registers than almost anyone. If you want a particular flavour, here is where it lives.

modes.b: The Lee/Kirby imperial phase — a genuinely new idea every month, and the highest density of things-that-still-matter in Marvel's history.
Byrne's five years, and Waid's after them. Marriage, children, a team member quitting because he is miserable. The FF as a family that argues.
Galactus and the Negative Zone in the 60s; the Council of Reeds and the multiverse in Hickman's. Both are about scale putting the family in perspective.
Hickman: planned years out, structured like a novel, and fundamentally about whether Reed Richards is a good man. Demands attention and repays it.
Millar and Hitch doing widescreen blockbuster — enormous set pieces, photo-real crowds, staged for a cinema screen.
Fraction and Allred. Pop-art line work, a substitute team, and a book about babysitting super-genius children. Nothing else here looks like it.
Fifteen years of Doom assembled in one place. The clearest demonstration that Marvel's best antagonist is a man with a point.
The Thing's own book — wrestling, Yancy Street, and Ben Grimm as a guy from the neighbourhood rather than a monster.
Ultimate FF: no continuity, young cast, modern pacing. The version to hand someone who has never read a comic.

ff-o1.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 1
ff-o1.lede: The first Marvel comic, and it takes a while to work out that is what it is. Watch a publisher stop making monster books and start making the modern superhero.

body: No costumes for three issues. No secret identities ever. A team who genuinely dislike each other, and a leader the book is willing to say is at fault. Every one of those was unusual in 1961 and together they are the beginning of Marvel's personality.

The early issues still read like the monster comics Kirby had been drawing the month before — giant creatures, subterranean kingdoms, alien invasions — and the pleasure of this volume is watching the superhero book displace them issue by issue.
Doom arrives in #5 and changes what a Marvel villain can be: a peer, a rival intellect, a monarch, and someone whose motivation is wounded pride.

fig.cap: Left: #1 — a monster and a rope. Right: #5, three issues later, and the genre has changed.

body: Read universally as essential history and uneven comics. The consensus is that the first ten or so issues are rough and fascinating, and that the book becomes genuinely great somewhere in the twenties — which is roughly when Kirby stops drawing monsters and starts designing a universe.

The Thing is the character readers single out here. He is much angrier and sadder in these issues than his later friendly-uncle version, and that early bitterness is the emotional engine of the whole run.

ff-o2.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 2
ff-o2.lede: The best three years any superhero comic has had. Galactus, the Silver Surfer, the Inhumans, the Negative Zone, the Black Panther — all of it, in about thirty issues.

body: It is worth stating the density plainly, because it sounds like exaggeration. In this volume Lee and Kirby introduce Galactus, the Silver Surfer, the Inhumans, the Negative Zone, the Black Panther and Wyatt Wingfoot, and produce the wedding of Reed and Sue. Most creative teams do not manage that in a career.

#48–50 is the Galactus trilogy, and the thing to notice is that it is not won by force. The threat is a god who is not malicious, and the resolution is moral rather than physical — which was a genuinely new shape for a superhero story.

#51, This Man... This Monster!, is the single issue most often named the finest superhero comic ever published. It is quiet, it is about envy and self-worth, and its climax is a stranger choosing to die well.

makers.b: Look for the collage pages in the Negative Zone material — actual photographs and cut paper pasted into the artwork because Kirby wanted a place that did not look drawn. It is the most avant-garde thing in mainstream 1960s comics and it is sitting in the middle of a superhero book.

Compare an issue before Sinnott arrives with one after. His rounded, high-gloss finish is what turned Kirby's raw power into something that looked expensive, and it defined the Marvel house look for a decade.

fig.cap: Left: #48. Right: #51 — no fight on the cover, and it is the best issue in the box.

body: As close to a settled verdict as comics criticism produces. This stretch is routinely named the greatest sustained run in superhero comics, and #51 in particular turns up at or near the top of best-single-issue lists decade after decade.

The honest caveat is the dialogue. Lee's scripting is enormously over-written by modern standards — everything is announced, nothing is implied — and readers coming from contemporary comics often need a few issues to tune to it. The plotting and the drawing are what have not dated.

ff-o3.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 3
ff-o3.lede: The last of Kirby, and it is still extraordinary — plus Annihilus, Franklin Richards, and a partnership visibly coming apart.

body: The invention does not stop — Annual #6 alone gives you Annihilus and the birth of Franklin Richards — but the book changes temperature. Kirby was increasingly unhappy about credit and ownership, and by the end he was, by his own account, deliberately holding his best ideas back.

He left after #102 in 1970 and went to DC. Knowing that is coming makes this volume read differently: it is the last stretch of the most important creative partnership in American comics, and both men knew it was ending.

fig.cap: Left: Annual #6 — Annihilus and Franklin in one book. Right: #102, the last one.

body: Rated just below Vol. 2 and comfortably above everything after it. The individual high points — Annual #6, the Inhumans material, the Doom stories — are as good as anything in the run.

The recurring observation is that the volume is less consistent than the one before it, with a noticeable drop in the last stretch. Whether you read that as Kirby losing interest or as Lee's scripting no longer matching him is the argument, and both parties have partisans.

ff-o4.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 4
ff-o4.lede: Life after Kirby, which turns out to be John Buscema drawing beautifully and the book quietly working out that it is now a legacy title.

body: The obvious move would have been to hire a Kirby imitator. Marvel hired John Buscema instead, who draws in a completely different register — classical, anatomically grounded, closer to illustration than to Kirby's engineering — and the book is better for the honesty.

What it loses is the invention rate. Nothing here has the density of the previous two volumes and the book knows it; it starts leaning on its own back catalogue, which is a thing no Marvel title had been old enough to do before.

makers.b: Watch the figures in repose. Buscema draws people standing and sitting better than almost anyone of his generation — real weight, real anatomy — where Kirby's genius was motion and force. The quiet pages are where the change is most visible.

body: Generally described as a good comic in the shadow of a great one, which is fair and slightly unkind. Buscema's art gets consistent praise and is often the reason people rate the volume at all.
The frequent complaint is that the stories are safe — a run consolidating rather than building. Readers who come to it directly after Vol. 3 tend to be harsher than readers who come to it on its own.

ff-o5.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 5
ff-o5.lede: The 1970s properly: a rotating cast of writers, real soap-opera plotting, and a team that spends a lot of this volume broken up.

sections.h: The book gets messy on purpose
body: Roy Thomas and then Gerry Conway push the domestic material much harder than Lee ever did — Reed and Sue separate, the team changes membership, and the problems do not resolve inside an issue.

This is the Bronze Age doing what it did everywhere at Marvel: taking the Silver Age's furniture and asking what it would actually be like to live in it. The results here are uneven and the intent is interesting.
Medusa joins the team, which is the era's best structural idea — replacing Sue with someone the others have to negotiate with rather than trust.
The least-discussed volume on the shelf, and the reception is mild rather than hostile: competent 1970s superhero comics with a few good stretches.

What defenders point to is the willingness to break the team up and leave it broken for a while, which no other era had tried. What detractors point to is a revolving door of writers and a book without a clear voice.

ff-o6.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 6
ff-o6.lede: The late Bronze Age, George Pérez arriving, and the issue where the Fantastic Four visit the Marvel offices and ask Stan Lee for a plot.

sections.h: Pérez, and a book that knows it is a book
body: George Pérez is the reason to read this volume. The FF suits him perfectly — four characters with four completely different rendering problems, a lot of machinery, and crowd scenes he can fill with specific faces.
#176 is the era's oddity and its most charming issue: the team goes to the Marvel Comics offices and interacts with the staff. It is a joke the book had earned by being fifteen years old.
Note that #171 was missing from the wiki's contents and has been restored by hand on this shelf — the volume's own solicit settles it.

makers.b: Density that stays readable. Pérez packs a page without confusing the reading path, and he draws machinery with real mechanical logic — the quality Todd McFarlane singled him out for, and it is on show throughout this book.

fig.cap: #176. The premise of the cover is that the comic is a comic.

body: Sits in the shadow of the Kirby and Byrne runs and is regularly rediscovered by readers working through the shelf in order. Pérez's issues are the draw, and they hold up completely.
The criticism is continuity of vision — four writers pass through and the book changes direction more than once. #176 is the issue people remember, and it is genuinely delightful.

byrne-o1.title: Fantastic Four by John Byrne Omnibus Vol. 1
byrne-o1.lede: One person writing and drawing the book for the first time since Kirby, and the run that decided what the modern Fantastic Four is.

body: Byrne's method is to go back through twenty years of the book, find what Lee and Kirby left unfinished, and finish it. The Negative Zone becomes a real place. Galactus gets a philosophy. Sue Richards stops being the weakest member and becomes the most powerful, which is the single most consequential character fix anyone has made here.
#258 is a day in Doctor Doom's life in Latveria with the FF barely in it, and it is one of the great villain stories in comics.

The other half of the run is domestic: a marriage under strain, a child who is a problem, and a Thing who eventually quits because he is unhappy. Byrne treats the book as a family drama with a rocket in it.

makers.b: Look at the panel grids. Byrne is unusually disciplined — regular layouts, deliberate panel counts, splash pages withheld until they land. That control is why the quiet issues work as well as the loud ones.

fig.cap: Left: #232, Byrne's first. Right: #258.

body: Universally treated as the best FF run after Lee and Kirby, and the only one usually mentioned in the same sentence. The Sue Richards material and the Doom issues are the specific things readers name.
The criticism that has grown over time is about tone drift in the later stretch — the run gets darker and more punishing in ways some readers find unearned. Vol. 1 is the less contested half.

thing-o1.title: Thing Omnibus
thing-o1.lede: Ben Grimm's own book, on the shelf because it is where his story actually goes when he quits the team — and because it is a different genre from everything around it.

body: The Thing works as a solo lead for a reason the FF book cannot use: he is the only member of the team who is not a scientist. Take him out of the Baxter Building and you have a guy from Yancy Street with a job and a temper.

The best-remembered stretch is the wrestling material — genuinely a sports comic, on the unarmoured Marvel Earth — and the Yancy Street issues, which are the closest Marvel came to a working-class New York book in the 1980s.
It sits between the two Byrne volumes on this shelf because that is where it belongs chronologically: Byrne Vol. 1 ends with Ben leaving the team, and this is where he goes.

fig.cap: The Thing #1, 1983 — a rock man standing in rubble with his name in big letters. No team, no logo.

body: A quiet, persistent favourite rather than a famous one. Readers who like it like it a great deal, and the reason is consistently the same: it is the only Marvel book of its era about somebody with a normal life and a bad attitude.

The reservations are that it is uneven across eight years and several creative teams, and that the wrestling arc — which is the part people remember fondly — is also the part furthest from what most readers pick up a Fantastic Four omnibus for. It is on the shelf because the user asked for it, and it earns the place.

byrne-o2.title: Fantastic Four by John Byrne Omnibus Vol. 2
byrne-o2.lede: The back half of the Byrne run — She-Hulk on the team, the darkest material anyone had put in this book, and an ending Byrne did not get to write.

body: With the Thing gone, She-Hulk joins, which works far better than it sounds — she is funny, she is enormous, and the team dynamic genuinely changes.

This is also the run's hardest stretch. #267 is the miscarriage issue, and there is a long sequence of Sue being psychically corrupted into Malice that has been argued about ever since. Byrne is pushing the family drama into places the book had never gone, and readers split on whether it earns them.
The run ends abruptly at #295 — Byrne left over editorial disagreements, and the finish is not the one he had planned.

fig.cap: #267. The cover asks what is the true cost of a man's mistakes? and it is not being rhetorical.

body: Rated highly and less comfortably than Vol. 1. The craft is not in question; what is argued about is how dark the run gets and whether the Malice and miscarriage material is handled well — readers genuinely disagree, and the disagreement is about substance rather than taste.

The She-Hulk period is much better liked than anyone expected in 1984 and is often the thing readers report enjoying most. The abrupt ending is a real frustration: the run stops rather than concludes.

waid-o1.title: Fantastic Four by Waid & Wieringo Omnibus
waid-o1.lede: The best modern FF, and the one where the readers got a creative team un-fired.

body: Waid's brief was straightforward and it had not been executed properly in years: they are explorers and they are a family. Not celebrities, not a corporation, not a dysfunctional soap. The book is funny, generous and interested in wonder.

Unthinkable is the run's landmark, and it works by moving Doom out of engineering and into sorcery — a villain who has decided that magic will get him what science did not. It is genuinely frightening in a way Doom had not been for twenty years.

Mike Wieringo is the other half of it: a light, animated, enormously expressive line, closer to animation design than to superhero rendering, and the reason the book reads as warm rather than nostalgic.

makers.b: Look at faces mid-sentence. Wieringo's characters act constantly — eyebrows, mouth corners, shoulders — which lets Waid write comedy that would die under a heavier artist. He died in 2007 at 44, and this run is the work he is remembered for.

fig.cap: Left: the nine-cent first issue. Right: #500, the Unthinkable climax.

body: Midway through, Marvel's then-president removed Waid and Wieringo from the book over a creative disagreement. The news broke online, the reaction was severe enough that the site reporting it went down under the traffic, and within weeks both were reinstated.
It is one of very few occasions on which a readership visibly reversed a publishing decision at Marvel, and it is part of why this run has the affection it does.

Very widely named the best Fantastic Four since Byrne, and frequently the recommendation for a modern reader who wants to know why this team matters. Unthinkable is treated as one of the definitive Doom stories.

Criticism is scarce and mostly amounts to it is not trying to be as ambitious as Hickman, which is true and beside the point. Wieringo's death has given the run an elegiac quality it did not have at the time.

millar-o1.title: Fantastic Four by Millar & Hitch Omnibus
millar-o1.lede: Widescreen. Enormous set pieces drawn at maximum detail, and the FF treated as a blockbuster franchise rather than a family.

body: Bryan Hitch's approach — photo-referenced crowds, panels shaped like film frames, huge double-page establishing shots — had already reshaped Marvel through The Ultimates, and this is it applied to the First Family.
Mark Millar writes to it: high-concept, high-velocity ideas, one enormous hook per arc. It is the least intimate FF run on the shelf and the most immediately spectacular.
Whether that is the right register for these characters is exactly the argument the run generates.

fig.cap: Hitch composes for a screen — note the framing and the depth of field, which are cinema conventions rather than comics ones.

body: Splits along a clean line. Readers who want scale and momentum rate it highly; readers who come to the FF for the family find it cold and impersonal, and that is the criticism that recurs.

Hitch's art is not much argued about — the draughtsmanship is extraordinary, and the run is worth having on the shelf for it. The complaint that does stick is pacing: Hitch's detail level caused delays, and the run reads as slightly unfinished.

hick-o1.title: Fantastic Four by Jonathan Hickman Omnibus Vol. 1
hick-o1.lede: The most ambitious thing anyone has done with these characters: a run planned years out, about whether Reed Richards' arrogance is the problem the book has been avoiding.

body: Hickman's opening premise is Reed joining a council of alternate versions of himself who have all set out to solve everything. It is a science-fiction idea and a character critique at once: every Reed in that room made the same choice, and most of them are monsters.

The construction is the thing to notice. Plot points seeded twenty issues ahead, diagrams and data pages between chapters, a genuinely novelistic shape. It rewards reading in a book far more than it did monthly.
#587 is where a member of the team dies, and Marvel shipped it polybagged. The issue after it is a silent one.

makers.b: Epting came from Brubaker's Captain America and brings that book's weight and shadow — grounded figures, heavy blacks, restrained staging. Against Hickman's cosmic material it is a deliberate mismatch that makes the scale feel real.

fig.cap: Left: Hickman's first issue. Right: #587 — black, and a numeral.

body: Frequently named the best FF run of the 21st century and one of the best Marvel runs of its generation. The specific praise is for structure and for taking Reed seriously as a moral problem rather than a plot device.

The recurring criticism is that it is demanding — slow to start, heavy on setup, and reliant on the reader holding a lot in their head. Several readers report bouncing off it monthly and loving it collected, which is what this shelf is for.

hick-o2.title: Fantastic Four by Jonathan Hickman Omnibus Vol. 2
hick-o2.lede: The payoff. Everything the first volume set up arrives at once, and the book becomes FF as well as Fantastic Four.

body: After #587 the title splits: FF runs alongside Fantastic Four, and the two are one continuous story. That is why this volume interleaves them.
The Future Foundation — a school for gifted children including several of Marvel's young villains — is the run's best invention and the thing later writers have kept.

The ending is the argument for the whole thing: threads laid down thirty issues earlier close simultaneously, which is very rare in ongoing superhero comics and is the specific pleasure Hickman is offering.
Rated alongside or slightly above Vol. 1, on the grounds that the payoff justifies the setup — which is the whole test for a run built this way.

The criticism is that the two-book structure makes it harder to follow than it needs to be, and that the Future Foundation children get more space than some readers want from a Fantastic Four comic. Both are fair; neither is common.

frac-o1.title: Fantastic Four by Matt Fraction Omnibus
frac-o1.lede: The family goes on a time-travelling holiday and a substitute team babysits. The strangest, prettiest and most divisive book on the shelf.

body: Fantastic Four is the road-trip book — Mark Bagley drawing the family across time and space. FF is the one that matters: a substitute team (Ant-Man, She-Hulk, Medusa and a pop star) minding the Future Foundation children, drawn by Michael Allred.

Allred's work here is genuinely unlike anything else Marvel was publishing — flat colour, clean mid-century line, pop-art composition. Laura Allred's colouring is half the effect. It looks like a 1965 advertisement and it is 2013.
Fraction has said he found the substitute book easier and more rewarding to write than the flagship, and it shows in both.

makers.b: Look at the flatness. Allred refuses rendering — no cross-hatch, no gradient, everything described by clean outline and solid colour. In a decade of heavy digital painting that reads as a deliberate argument, and it makes every page instantly legible.

fig.cap: The 2012 relaunch. Bagley on the flagship; the Allred book is the one people kept.

body: The two halves are received very differently, which is the key thing to know. The FF substitute-team book with Allred has a devoted following and is called one of the best things Marvel published that decade by the people who love it.

The flagship Fantastic Four half gets a much cooler reception: the recurring words are convoluted and tonally inconsistent, the time travel is called unnecessarily confusing, and following Hickman did it no favours.
Read the Allred issues first. If the whimsy works for you, the rest will.

slott-o1.title: Fantastic Four by Dan Slott Omnibus Vol. 1
slott-o1.lede: The team comes back after three years off the shelf entirely, and the brief is simply: make it warm again.

body: The Fantastic Four had been cancelled — no title at all from 2015 to 2018, the longest absence since 1961. Slott's relaunch is unashamedly restorative: get the family back together, get Ben and Alicia married, make the book feel like the thing people remember.

It is the least formally ambitious era on the shelf and it is doing that on purpose. After Hickman's architecture and Fraction's experiment, a straight-ahead warm Fantastic Four comic is a real position.
The one-shots threaded through the run — the wedding special, 4 Yancy Street, the Negative Zone book — are why this volume is chaptered per book rather than as numbered parts.

fig.cap: 2018. The cover is the logo and the four of them, which is the entire editorial thesis.

body: Liked rather than celebrated, and that seems to be roughly what it was aiming for. The consistent praise is for getting the voices right and for treating the team as a family again after several years of not existing.

The criticism is that it is safe — readers looking for the ambition of the Hickman years find it slight. The wedding issue and the Doom material are the parts most often singled out as better than the run's reputation.

slott-o2.title: Fantastic Four by Dan Slott Omnibus Vol. 2
slott-o2.lede: The back half — bigger, stranger, and more willing to break things than the first.

body: With the restoration done, the run gets more adventurous: Reed and Doom's relationship gets a proper reckoning, the Bentley and Valeria material comes forward, and the scale of the stories goes up considerably.
It is still recognisably the same warm book — nobody is going to mistake this for Hickman — but the second volume takes risks the first deliberately did not.
Rated slightly above Vol. 1 by most readers, on the grounds that the run found its confidence once it no longer had to prove the family worked.
The reception is quiet overall. This is a well-made, well-liked, unfashionable run, and its main critical problem is being the fourth act after three much-discussed ones.

doom-o1.title: Doctor Doom: The Book of Doom Omnibus
doom-o1.lede: Fifteen years of Marvel's best villain, assembled out of everyone else's comics. Read it and the whole shelf reads differently.

body: Doom works because he is not evil in the way villains were in 1962. He is a head of state, a scientist of genuine rank, and a man whose entire motivation is that Reed Richards was right about something once.

Read chronologically and out of the FF's context, the thing that emerges is how often the book agrees with him. He is right about Reed's arrogance; he is right about the FF's carelessness; he is wrong only ever about himself.
The volume doubles back across the numbered omnibuses above — a lot of its contents are also in those books, and marking an issue here marks it there.
Judged as a collection decision, and a good one: gathering Doom's appearances chronologically produces a genuine character study that no single run contains.

The reservation is the overlap — a substantial share of this book is already in the numbered volumes, so its value depends on whether you want the through-line badly enough to buy the duplication. Readers who do, tend to rate it very highly indeed.

uff-o1.title: Ultimate Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 1
uff-o1.lede: Restart them as teenagers in a government think tank. The most accessible version of the concept anyone has made, and the accidental birthplace of Marvel Zombies.

body: The Ultimate line's central move — strip the continuity, lower the ages, raise the pacing — suits the FF unusually well, because the original premise is already about clever people out of their depth.
Bendis and Millar alternate on the writing and Adam Kubert draws the early issues with a real sense of scale. It is a good superhero comic that assumes nothing.
It also produced the strangest spin-off in modern Marvel: Millar and Greg Land's zombie-universe arc turned into Marvel Zombies, which nobody planned and which outsold most of the line.

fig.cap: Ultimate FF #1 — young, modern, and designed for a reader with no history at all.

body: Regarded as one of the better Ultimate books without being one of the great ones. The consistent recommendation is as an entry point: it is genuinely the easiest book on this shelf to hand to a new reader.
The criticism is that it never quite develops an identity beyond the Fantastic Four, but younger — where Ultimate Spider-Man and The Ultimates both found their own reasons to exist.

uff-o2.title: Ultimate Fantastic Four Omnibus Vol. 2
uff-o2.lede: The back half of the Ultimate run, where it stops being an introduction and starts damaging its own cast.

body: The Ultimate universe as a whole got considerably harsher after 2006, and this book goes with it. Mike Carey's stretch in particular is far bleaker than anything in the first volume, and the cast take real damage.
It is a better-written book than Vol. 1 and a less inviting one, which is the trade-off the whole Ultimate line made in its second half.

Reception is softer than Vol. 1's. The writing is generally considered stronger and the tone considerably less fun, and readers who came for the accessible version report the second volume being a different book.
The Carey issues have real defenders. The overall verdict is that the run ends having lost the thing that made it worth starting.
